item.title: Big Read: Kenya is targeting a fourteen-night stay. Google's new hotel bid cannot tell one night from fourteen.
item.description: A grey box at the top of Google's documentation says hotel campaigns migrate to Search campaigns for Travel from the fourth quarter of 2026. Three bid types do not come with them, including the one that set a bid as a percentage of the room price and multiplied it by the length of stay. East Africa sells the high-rate, long-duration stay that bid was built to price, and almost nobody at the lodges

item.title: Big Read: One oven at Nungwi burned six hotels. Zanzibar inspects one building at a time.
item.description: A bread oven at the Makofi hotel caught at about 2.20pm on Saturday. Three hours later six hotels, four restaurants and some forty shops on Zanzibar's busiest beach had stopped being businesses. This is the fourth multiple-property fire on an East African thatched strip since 2017, and it is not a building failure. It is a failure to regulate the space between buildings, inside an insurance market

item.title: Big Read: Uganda counted 1.6 million visitors last year. Its holiday arrivals grew by 0.4 per cent.
item.description: The World Bank's November tourism brief puts Uganda down 7 per cent on the quarter while Rwanda is up 19. Uganda's own ministry says arrivals rose 3.7 per cent in the same half-year, its civil aviation authority says air traffic fell 10.8 per cent, and its park gates counted 7.9 per cent fewer people. All four numbers are real. Only one of them describes the market a lodge sells into.

item.title: Big Read: India got a daily flight to Tanzania this morning. The guest on it is worth $276 a night less.
item.description: IndiGo's first daily Mumbai to Dar es Salaam service was scheduled to land at 06:05 today, and India entered Tanzania's mainland top fifteen source markets for the first time last year. But package visitors spent $479 a night on the mainland in 2025 and non-package visitors spent $203. item.title: Big Read: Uganda has cut the gorilla permit price in April, May and November. May was its busiest month of the year.
item.description: A short table in Uganda Wildlife Authority's January 2027 tariff knocks 200 dollars off a gorilla permit in three named months. The Ministry of Tourism's own half-year statistics show one of those months was the single busiest for arrivals, while half the permit book went unsold all year. The discount is keyed to the calendar, and the problem is not calendar-shaped.

item.title: Big Read: Kenya is first on the list for a levy on business class arrivals. The row of numbers behind it does not add up.
item.description: A COP31 declaration launched in Antalya on Tuesday welcomed small levies on polluting sectors, with Kenya among its backers. Four days earlier the task force Kenya co-chairs published the modelling, and Kenya came first of ten countries at $84 million a year. Work the report's own published figures back and the Kenya row implies a revenue base roughly four times the passenger base it uses to count

item.title: Big Read: Tanzania doubled the beds inside its national parks. The 160 sites it has just put on the market are in the parks nobody flies to.
item.description: TANAPA's annual results, released on 10 November, show in-park bed capacity up from 5,755 to 12,094 since 2021, a revenue target missed by about 66 billion shillings, and domestic park visits down 7.7 per cent in a single year. The agency's answer is 160 more investment sites, 130 of them camps, concentrated in a circuit whose access project the government itself asked the World Bank to cancel.

item.title: Big Read: Uganda's shilling fell 16 per cent this year. Rwanda's franc fell 2. The same dollar rate card now means four different things.
item.description: For two decades East Africa's dollar-priced hotels carried an automatic hedge: when local costs rose, the local currency fell, and the gap closed itself. In 2026 that stopped working in half the region, and Rwanda's October inflation print shows what a property is left holding when it does.

item.title: Big Read: Zanzibar's hotels have five weeks to install CCTV. Nobody has produced the order.
item.description: Three accounts published in two days gave the archipelago's hotels a 15 December deadline, a camera specification and a schedule of penalties. None of them cites a circular, a gazette notice or a named official, and they disagree on the one question that decides the price.
